notes.h: Types of leisure facility in the community (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Leisure facilities are provided by public bodies, commercial businesses and voluntary groups, and each type is funded and run differently.
points: Public facilities are provided by local authorities and include swimming pools, leisure centres, libraries, parks, playgrounds and sports pitches.
Commercial facilities are run for profit and include gyms, private health clubs, cinemas, bowling alleys and golf clubs.
Voluntary and community facilities are run by non-profit groups and include GAA clubs, tennis clubs, community centres and youth clubs.
Public facilities are funded mainly by local authority budgets and user charges, and their fees are set by the provider.
Commercial facilities depend on fees from users for their income, so the fee charged must cover running costs and make a profit.
Voluntary facilities depend on volunteers and member subscriptions, so their range and condition vary from club to club.

notes.h: Criteria for evaluating a leisure facility (Higher Level only)
notes.b: An evaluation judges a facility against fixed criteria, so that two facilities can be compared on the same basis.
points: Cost: the fees charged, judged against what the user can afford.
Value: the benefits the user gains from the facility, judged against its cost.
Accessibility: the ease of reaching the facility and using it, including location, transport and access for people with disabilities.
Range of facilities: the number and variety of activities, such as pools, classes, courts or equipment, that the facility offers.
Convenience: whether the opening hours and booking arrangements suit the user's working and family pattern.
Safety and hygiene: the cleanliness of changing areas and equipment, supervision, and emergency procedures.
Staffing: the qualifications of instructors and lifeguards, and the level of supervision during sessions.
Social benefits: the opportunity to meet people and join groups, classes or teams.
Physical, emotional and intellectual benefits: the gains in fitness, relaxation and skill that the facility makes possible.
Location: a facility close to home or work reduces travel time and cost, and is more likely to be used regularly.
Transport: the availability of buses or trains and the provision of parking affect how easily a user can get there.
Access for people with disabilities: ramps, lifts, accessible changing rooms and pool hoists allow people with mobility difficulties to use the facility.
Opening hours: early, late and weekend hours suit people who work or attend school during the day.
Booking systems: online booking and advance booking of classes make it easier to plan use, while queues and walk-in only systems can discourage use.
Family access: facilities that allow children and adults to use the same area together make family leisure easier to organise.

notes.h: Cost of using a facility (Higher Level only)
points: Membership fee: a regular fee, usually paid monthly or yearly, that gives unlimited or extended use of the facility.
Joining fee: a one-off payment made when a person first becomes a member of a facility.
Pay-as-you-go charge: a fee paid each time the facility is used, which suits people who visit only occasionally.
Class and course fees: extra charges for instructor-led sessions, which are often separate from the basic entry or membership fee.
Concessions: reduced fees for students, children, older people and unemployed people, which lower the cost for these groups.
Hidden costs: travel, equipment, clothing and locker or towel hire add to the total cost of using a facility.
Total annual cost: the sum of membership or joining fees, pay-as-you-go charges, class fees and travel for one year.

notes.h: Value and value for money (Higher Level only)
points: Value is the benefit a person gains from a facility, measured in fitness, enjoyment, social contact and skill.
Value for money is the benefit gained for each euro spent, so a cheap facility that is rarely used may offer poor value.
A facility offers more value when its range of activities matches the user's interests, and when the user actually uses those activities.
Cost per visit is found by dividing the total annual cost by the number of visits made in the year.
A low cost per visit shows that the facility is used often, which generally means better value for regular users.
Value depends on the user: a person who uses only the pool may find a high-fee gym poor value, even though it offers more activities.

notes.h: Cost and value comparison of two facilities (Higher Level only)
points: Step 1: select two facilities that serve the same community and are used for the same purpose, such as fitness or swimming.
Step 2: find each facility's fees: membership, joining, pay-as-you-go and class fees.
Step 3: calculate the total annual cost of each facility, including the travel cost of getting there.
Step 4: estimate the number of visits per year for the user, and divide the total annual cost by that number to find the cost per visit.
Step 5: list the benefits each facility gives the user, including fitness, social contact, relaxation and skill, and compare them with the cost.
Step 6: state which facility gives better value for the user, and say what would change the conclusion, such as a change in visits or income.

notes.h: Evaluation judgement and improvements (Higher Level only)
points: An evaluation weighs the strengths of each facility against its weaknesses, then reaches a judgement for a named type of user.
A facility with low fees but few activities may suit a student who wants cheap exercise, but not a family wanting varied activities.
Improvements a facility could make include extended opening hours, reduced fees for families and older people, and better access for people with disabilities.
Improvements to booking and information, such as online timetables, make a facility easier to use and so raise its value.

keyTerms.definition: A leisure facility provided and run by a local authority or other public body, such as a swimming pool or library.
A leisure facility run for profit, such as a private gym, cinema or golf club.
A leisure facility run by a non-profit group or club, such as a GAA club or community centre.
A regular payment that gives a person continued use of a leisure facility.
A system in which a user pays a fee each time they use a facility, rather than a membership fee.
A reduced fee offered to a group such as students, children, older people or unemployed people.
The ease with which a facility can be reached and used, including by people with disabilities.
The benefit gained from a facility in relation to the cost of using it.
The total annual cost of a facility divided by the number of visits made in the year.
A one-off payment made when a person first joins a leisure facility as a member.

factCards.term: Three types of leisure facility in a community
factCards.definition: 1. Public facilities, such as swimming pools, leisure centres and libraries. 2. Commercial facilities, such as gyms, cinemas and golf clubs. 3. Voluntary or community facilities, such as GAA clubs and community centres.

factCards.term: Four criteria for evaluating a leisure facility
factCards.definition: 1. Cost and value. 2. Accessibility. 3. Range of activities. 4. Safety, hygiene and staffing.

factCards.term: Two types of charge a leisure facility makes
factCards.definition: 1. Fixed charges, such as a membership fee or joining fee. 2. Variable charges, such as pay-as-you-go fees, class fees and equipment hire.

factCards.term: Three ways to improve the accessibility of a leisure facility
factCards.definition: 1. Extend opening hours to early mornings, evenings and weekends. 2. Offer concessions for families and older people. 3. Provide access for people with disabilities, such as ramps, lifts and accessible changing rooms.
The total annual cost of using the facility divided by the number of visits made in the year.

questions.prompt: Explain how to calculate the cost per visit of a leisure facility and state why this figure is useful when comparing two facilities.
questions.model: Calculation: add the membership or joining fees, pay-as-you-go charges, class fees and travel costs for one year to find the total annual cost, then divide that total by the number of visits made in the year. Usefulness: it allows two facilities with different fee structures to be compared on the same basis, and it shows whether a facility gives good value to a regular user. Both the method and the reason are needed for full marks.

questions.prompt: Evaluate two leisure facilities in your community, including a cost and value comparison. Refer to accessibility and the range of activities, and recommend which facility gives better value to a family of four.
questions.model: Two facilities identified, one public and one commercial or voluntary. Cost: fees for membership, joining, pay-as-you-go and classes, plus travel, totalled for one year and divided by the expected number of family visits to give cost per visit. Value: the benefits each facility gives, such as physical fitness, social contact and skill development for each family member, weighed against cost. Accessibility: location, transport, opening hours, booking arrangements and access for people with disabilities. Range of activities: whether the facility offers activities suited to all ages in the family, and whether they can be used together. Recommendation: the facility giving the lower cost per visit and the wider benefit for the family, with the reason stated and any improvements suggested, such as concessions for families or extended opening hours.
